assessment:
In this study, Turi and colleagues investigate the activity patterns of dentate gyrus (DG) neurons during sleep-wake cycles in mice, with a focus on understanding how serotonergic neuromodulation shapes these patterns during non-REM (NREM) sleep. The authors employ a combination of fiber photometry, two-photon calcium imaging, EEG/EMG recordings, and genetic manipulations to characterize neuronal dynamics and their relationship to sleep microarchitecture. The work addresses an important gap in our understanding of how the dentate gyrus—the input gateway to the hippocampus—operates during sleep, and how neuromodulatory systems organize this activity.

The key findings are well-supported by multiple complementary approaches. Using fiber photometry in genetically defined cell populations, the authors demonstrate that both granule cells and mossy cells exhibit an infraslow oscillation (ISO) at 0.01-0.03 Hz during NREM sleep, a novel observation not previously reported in the DG. Two-photon imaging reveals that approximately 50% of granule cells and 28% of mossy cells are upregulated during NREM compared to wakefulness, and these cells drive the population-level oscillation. Critically, dual-site photometry recordings establish that DG activity and raphe serotonergic activity are anticorrelated during NREM sleep, oscillating at matching frequencies but in opposite phases. The troughs of the DG oscillation precede microarousals by approximately 6 seconds, suggesting a predictive relationship. Genetic knockdown of Htr1a receptors in the DG disrupts the ISO and impairs contextual fear memory, providing mechanistic evidence that serotonin acts via inhibitory Htr1a receptors to pace the oscillation. The experimental design is rigorous, with appropriate controls including verification of receptor knockdown by in situ hybridization and demonstration that sleep architecture remains intact despite the manipulation.

While the correlation between serotonergic activity and DG oscillations is convincing, and the Htr1a manipulation clearly affects both the oscillation and memory performance, the direct causal link between ISO disruption and memory impairment remains somewhat uncertain. The authors acknowledge this limitation, noting that the relationship between neuromodulatory effects on sleep activity and sleep-dependent memory consolidation requires further demonstration. Additionally, the ISO was not observed at the single-cell level in head-fixed two-photon imaging, which the authors attribute to differences in sleep depth or a predominantly dendritic origin of the signal—reasonable hypotheses that warrant future investigation. The study also raises intriguing questions about how multiple neuromodulatory systems (serotonin, norepinephrine, acetylcholine) coordinate to shape sleep microarchitecture, as recent work has shown similar infraslow oscillations in other neuromodulatory systems.

Overall, this work makes a substantial contribution to our understanding of dentate gyrus function during sleep and provides novel mechanistic insights into serotonergic modulation of hippocampal activity patterns. The findings will be of broad interest to researchers studying sleep, memory consolidation, hippocampal function, and neuromodulation. The rigorous methodology combining population-level recordings, cellular resolution imaging, and genetic manipulations strengthens confidence in the main conclusions, though the functional significance of the ISO for memory processes could benefit from more direct experimental evidence.
